clinicalPearls: In iodine-sufficient regions the most common causes are autoimmune disease (Hashimoto's thyroiditis) and iatrogenic injury (treatment of hyperthyroidism); iodine deficiency remains a leading cause worldwide (p.3027).
Biochemical hallmark of primary hypothyroidism is an elevated TSH with a low unbound (free) T4; a normal TSH excludes primary, but not secondary/central, disease (p.3030-3031).

Subclinical hypothyroidism is biochemical thyroid hormone deficiency (raised TSH, usually still-normal free T4) with few or no symptoms; overt hypothyroidism typically corresponds to TSH >10 mIU/L with a low free T4 (p.3029, p.3032).

Symptoms (descending frequency) include tiredness/weakness, dry skin, cold intolerance, hair loss, poor concentration and memory, constipation, and modest weight gain with poor appetite (the weight gain is mainly fluid retention in myxedematous tissue) (p.3028-3029).

Signs include dry coarse skin, cool extremities, nonpitting puffiness of face/hands/feet (myxedema), diffuse alopecia with thinning of the outer eyebrow, bradycardia, peripheral edema, and delayed relaxation of tendon reflexes (p.3028-3029).
TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies are present in >95% of autoimmune hypothyroidism and confirm the etiology once hypothyroidism is established (p.3030).

Onset is usually insidious, so patients may only recognize symptoms once euthyroidism is restored; Hashimoto's patients may present with goiter (irregular, firm) rather than hypothyroid symptoms (p.3029-3030).

Associated laboratory abnormalities include raised creatine phosphokinase, elevated cholesterol and triglycerides, and a normocytic or macrocytic anemia, which generally resolve with thyroxine replacement (p.3030).

Autoimmune hypothyroidism clusters with other autoimmune disorders, particularly vitiligo, pernicious anemia, Addison's disease (Schmidt's syndrome), type 1 diabetes, and the autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes (p.3030).
harrison.pathophysiology: Hypothyroidism is deficient thyroid hormone action, most often from primary thyroid failure. In autoimmune (Hashimoto's) disease, T cell-mediated lymphocytic infiltration with germinal-center formation, follicular atrophy, oxyphil metaplasia, and fibrosis progressively destroy the gland; atrophic thyroiditis represents its fibrotic end stage. As function declines there is a compensated phase in which a rising TSH maintains hormone levels (subclinical hypothyroidism); later free T4 falls and TSH rises further, producing overt disease. Susceptibility reflects genetic factors (HLA-DR3/DR4/DR5, PTPN22, CTLA-4) and environmental factors including high iodine intake. TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies are markers; up to 20% of patients have TSH-receptor-blocking antibodies that prevent TSH binding and can cause thyroid atrophy and, by transplacental passage, transient neonatal hypothyroidism. Increased dermal glycosaminoglycan deposition traps water, producing nonpitting myxedema (Harrison 22e p.3029-3030).
additionalDifferentials: Hyperthyroidism / thyrotoxicosis (opposite end of thyroid dysfunction; thyroiditis can pass through both phases)
Secondary (central) hypothyroidism from hypopituitarism or hypothalamic disease
Multinodular goiter or thyroid carcinoma (asymmetric Hashimoto goiter may mimic these)
Primary thyroid lymphoma (rare, strongly associated with pre-existing autoimmune thyroiditis)
Depression and dementia (overlapping fatigue, poor concentration, slowing)
additionalInvestigations: Serum TSH as the primary screening test (most sensitive for primary disease)
Free/unbound T4 to confirm clinical hypothyroidism when TSH is elevated (T3 measurement is not indicated)
TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies to establish autoimmune etiology
Lipid panel (cholesterol, triglycerides), creatine phosphokinase, and full blood count for associated abnormalities
Anterior pituitary function testing when central hypothyroidism is suspected (after excluding drug effect and sick euthyroid syndrome)
Thyroid ultrasound to distinguish heterogeneous Hashimoto echotexture from true nodules warranting FNA
redFlags: Myxedema coma — the severe end of untreated hypothyroidism: reduced level of consciousness (sometimes seizures), hypothermia (can reach 23 C), with 20-40% mortality despite treatment; almost always in the elderly and often precipitated by infection, cold, sedatives, or acute cardiopulmonary events.
Hypoventilation with hypoxia and hypercapnia, plus hypoglycemia and dilutional hyponatremia, in profound hypothyroidism.
Impaired adrenal reserve in profound hypothyroidism (consider co-existing adrenal insufficiency before/with thyroid replacement).
Neonatal/congenital hypothyroidism — risk of permanent neurologic damage if treatment is delayed, mandating neonatal screening.
Significant pericardial or other serous effusions, conductive deafness, or carpal tunnel/entrapment syndromes as manifestations of severe disease.
harrison.prognosis: With levothyroxine replacement and dose titration to a normal TSH, prognosis is excellent and most laboratory and clinical abnormalities resolve, though full symptomatic relief may take months and about 10-15% report persistent symptoms despite biochemical euthyroidism. Untreated congenital hypothyroidism causes permanent neurologic damage, and myxedema coma still carries a 20-40% mortality independent of T4 and TSH levels (Harrison 22e p.3031-3032).
pitfalls: Central (secondary) hypothyroidism is missed if TSH is used alone: in pituitary/hypothalamic disease TSH may be low, normal, or even slightly raised, so a low free T4 is needed to make the diagnosis and TSH cannot be used to monitor therapy.
A normal TSH excludes primary but NOT secondary/central hypothyroidism.
T4 alone is an inferior screening test because it will not detect subclinical hypothyroidism; T3 is normal in ~25% of patients and is not indicated.
An elevated TSH with normal/high free T4 in a patient on adequate levothyroxine usually reflects poor adherence (taking medication only shortly before testing), not a TSH-secretion disorder.
Confirm that a raised TSH is sustained over ~3 months before treating subclinical hypothyroidism.
TSH should not be relied on in the months immediately after radioiodine for Graves' disease (it stays suppressed); use unbound T4 instead.
External rewarming in myxedema coma can precipitate cardiovascular collapse, and hypotonic fluids can worsen hyponatremia.
harrison.severityClassification: Spectrum from subclinical hypothyroidism (raised TSH, normal free T4, few/no symptoms) to overt/clinical hypothyroidism (raised TSH usually >10 mIU/L with low free T4 and symptoms); myxedema coma represents the severe, life-threatening end. Etiologically classified as primary (thyroidal), secondary/central (pituitary or hypothalamic), congenital, or transient (Harrison 22e p.3027-3032).
management: Replace thyroid hormone with oral levothyroxine titrated to normalise TSH (or free thyroxine in central disease), taken on an empty stomach away from interfering foods and medicines
Start low and up-titrate slowly in the elderly and in those with ischaemic heart disease to avoid precipitating angina or arrhythmia
Ensure adequate glucocorticoid cover is established before starting levothyroxine where coexisting adrenal insufficiency is suspected in central hypothyroidism
Monitor TSH after dose changes and through pregnancy, when levothyroxine requirements rise

Treat myxoedema coma as an emergency with parenteral levothyroxine (with liothyronine in some protocols), parenteral glucocorticoid and supportive rewarming with ventilatory and haemodynamic support in critical care
Individualise treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism according to degree of TSH elevation, antibody status, symptoms and pregnancy plans
Screen for and manage associated autoimmune disease, and reassess the need for replacement when a reversible thyroiditis is the cause
